newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese opposition calls for general strike.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese opposition calls for general strike.

text.p: Lebanese opposition groups called on Tuesday for a general strike next week to protest against what they called "violations of freedom and democracy" by the government of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

The call for a strike and demonstration on November 28 followed criticism of a government decision to shut scores of private radio and television stations by November 30 under a law regulating those media for the first time.

It was issued by a committee representing a broad spectrum of opposition politicians, labour unions and media workers who last Friday held the biggest meeting against Hariri's policies since he became prime minister in October 1992.

The meeting demanded a five-month postponement in applying the law, cancellation of a ban on public demonstrations imposed by Hariri since 1993 and a series of changes to the government's economic and financial policies.
The strike call neatly upstaged Hariri, coming shortly after he read to parliament the policy statement of his new government formed on November 7, the third he has headed.
The billionaire construction tycoon responded to the last general strike by labour unions on February 29 by calling out the army, which slapped a curfew on most of the country.
Indicating he might do the same, Hariri told a conference of Arab bankers in Beirut earlier on Tuesday he would "hit with an iron fist any attempt to shake the stability (of the country)."

Hariri's statement to parliament went some way to answering critics who say his multibillion dollar reconstruction drive has ignored the needs of the poor, but it made no concessions on the media issue.

It said the new government would develop medicare, social security, education and public transport. It would also develop small and medium-sized industry, agriculture and tourism while ensuring Lebanon's economic, financial and social stability.

"The government's policy will remain unchanged in carrying out development projects, accelerating growth and increasing state revenues in order to strengthen the monetary and financial situation," the statement said.
It made no mention of the media law that has galvanised the opposition.

All opposition radio and television stations are to be closed under the law while most of the 15 broadcasting licences have been awarded to establishment figures like Hariri, other ministers and parliament Speaker Nabih Berri.

However, Hariri's support within the political establishment appeared to weaken on Tuesday when Berri authorised a protest sit-in against the law outside parliament next Monday when the house starts debating the government's policy statement.
Berri has said the problem is not the law itself but the way Hariri's government is applying it.
His effort to distance himself could cause Hariri concern about parliament's reaction when it holds a vote of confidence on the government's policy statement next week.

Hariri already faces opposition on the issue from a broad cross-section of opinion. Last Friday's opposition meeting was an unprecedented gathering of hitherto mutually hostile politicians, parties and movements, both Moslem and Christian.
